title: The Dirt Bike
author: Katherine Martinko
summary: A mother recounts her son spending a summer working at the family pizzeria to save up for a used dirt bike, and her mixed feelings — pride at his determination, fear for his safety riding logging roads alone — as she works to give him age-appropriate independence rather than fear-driven overprotection. The essay closes on him returning from a solo ride with wild raspberries, a small proof that letting go paid off.
points: Her son worked every shift he could at the family's wood-fired pizzeria to save enough for a used 125cc dirt bike within four weeks.
As a former environmental journalist, she's conflicted about the noisy, gas-burning bike, but values that it draws him deep into the forests she loves.
She equips him with practical skills and warnings (water, matches, a knife, a route) rather than trying to tether him to her out of fear.
She frames the tension as a broader parenting shift: balancing her own behavioral standards against giving an older child room to become himself.
The piece closes with him returning from a solo ride with a container of wild raspberries, a moment only possible because he was 'still going slowly enough to stop and notice.'

He concocted all sorts of illogical plans for getting one, until settling on the most obvious solution, which was to get a job, work hard, and save enough money to buy one.
It goes to show the power of having a personal goal, and how, when a person wants something badly enough, they’ll put themselves through significant hardship to achieve it.
I trust that his cautious, sensible nature will prevail. Then I have to let him go and trust that he’ll be fine.
I found a huge raspberry patch along the old highway! And there were places where I could tell bears had crushed the bushes, so I made lots of noise to make sure they were gone.
